content: Yersinia pestis is the bacterium responsible for causing the bubonic plague, also known as the Black Death. During the incubation period of the disease, characteristic swollen lymph nodes, known as buboes, typically develop in the armpits and groin. These buboes form because the bacteria localize and multiply in the lymph nodes. If left untreated, the infection can disseminate rapidly, leading to systemic involvement and affecting multiple organs. Yersinia pestis was historically classified under the Pasteurellaceae family. However, based on DNA-DNA hybridization studies showing similarities to Escherichia coli, it was reclassified in 1995 as part of the Enterobacteriaceae family. Members of this family are differentiated based on their biochemical and antigenic profiles. Advances in nucleic acid techniques have further refined the classification of Yersinia species. Among the 11 named species in the Yersinia genus, only three are significant human pathogens: Yersinia pestis, Yersinia pseudotuberculosis, and Yersinia enterocolitica. Yersinia pseudotuberculosis is the closest genetic relative to Yersinia pestis but can be distinguished by its clinical presentation and laboratory findings. While Yersinia enterocolitica is more commonly isolated in clinical specimens, Yersinia pestis and Yersinia pseudotuberculosis rarely infect humans. Yersinia pestis is highly infectious, requiring as few as 1 to 10 organisms to cause disease in small mammals, such as rodents or primates, through subcutaneous, oral, intravenous, or intradermal routes. However, respiratory transmission in nonhuman primates requires a higher infectious dose, approximately 100 to 200,000 organisms. Upon entering the host, the bacteria respond to various environmental signals, such as elevated temperature, low pH within cells, and contact with eukaryotic cells, which trigger the synthesis of virulence factors. During the incubation phase, the bacteria often spread to regional lymph nodes, leading to the formation of buboes, the hallmark symptom of bubonic plague. If untreated, the infection progresses rapidly, resulting in septicemia and dissemination to other organs. Septicemic plague is often associated with cyanosis and necrosis, which may be attributed to the coagulase activity of the plasminogen activator. Commonly affected tissues include the liver, lungs, skin, mucous membranes, spleen, and, in later stages, the meninges. Yersinia pestis is a Gram-negative, facultative anaerobic, bipolar-staining bacillus that belongs to the Enterobacteriaceae family. Its bipolar staining gives it a characteristic safety pin appearance under the microscope. The bacterium is capable of causing three clinical forms of plague: bubonic, pneumonic, and septicemic. Historically, these forms have been associated with high mortality rates, including during the Black Death, which killed approximately one-third of Europe’s population between 1347 and 1353. Yersinia pestis produces an antiphagocytic slime layer and exhibits motility when isolated in vitro, but it becomes nonmotile within the mammalian host. The pathogenicity of Yersinia pestis is partly due to two key antiphagocytic antigens, F1 (Fraction 1) and V, which are critical for its virulence. These antigens are produced at 37°C and allow the bacterium to evade phagocytosis. Yersinia pestis can survive and produce these antigens within monocytes but not within polymorphonuclear neutrophils. Immunity to the bacterium, whether natural or induced, involves the production of specific opsonic antibodies against the F1 and V antigens. These antibodies promote phagocytosis by neutrophils. Current research is focused on developing genetically engineered vaccines based on the F1 and V antigens. However, the variability of the V antigen and the virulence of F1-deficient strains present challenges to creating a fully protective vaccine. The complete genomic sequences of two Yersinia pestis subspecies, strain KIM (biovar Medievalis) and strain CO92 (biovar Orientalis), are available. The KIM strain has a chromosome length of 4,600,755 base pairs, while the CO92 strain has a chromosome length of 4,653,728 base pairs. A third subspecies, biovar Antiqua, has not yet been fully sequenced. Yersinia pestis harbors three plasmids: pCD1, pPCP1, and pMT1. The latter two plasmids are unique to Yersinia pestis and are not found in other Yersinia species. These plasmids, along with a pathogenicity island called HPI, encode proteins responsible for the bacterium’s virulence. These factors facilitate bacterial adhesion, injection of proteins into host cells, invasion of host cells, and acquisition of iron from red blood cells. Yersinia pestis is believed to have evolved from Yersinia pseudotuberculosis, with the primary difference being the acquisition of specific virulence plasmids. Recent proteomic analyses of Yersinia pestis strain KIM have provided insights into its adaptation to growth conditions mimicking those within host cells. The traditional first-line treatments for Yersinia pestis infections include streptomycin, chloramphenicol, tetracycline, and fluoroquinolones. Doxycycline and gentamicin are also effective options. However, antibiotic resistance has been observed in some strains, necessitating treatment guided by antibiotic susceptibility testing whenever possible.
